prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Justice Department officials blocked liberals and people with Democratic Party ties from a highly selective program that funneled young lawyers into government jobs, according to an internal investigation released Tuesday. A bias against liberals existed in a Justice program meant to hire young lawyers, an investigation found. Esther Slater McDonald, a political appointee at the Justice Department, "wrote disparaging statements about the candidates' liberal and Democratic Party affiliations on the applications she reviewed and ... she voted to deselect candidates on that basis," said the report by Inspector General Glenn Fine. McDonald, who has left the department, refused to be interviewed for the investigation. The report, the first official investigation to document politicization of the Justice Department during the Bush administration, is an offshoot of the larger investigation of Justice Department politics triggered by the furor over the firing of nine U.S. attorneys. It found two of three members of a screening committee considered political views and experience when choosing new lawyers for the Justice Department Honors Program and Summer Law Intern Program. The report found that McDonald and Michael Elston, the chief of staff to Deputy Attorney General Paul McNulty, engaged in misconduct, an administrative violation. The third member of the screening committee, career lawyer Dan Fridman, was cleared of any involvement in the politicization of the process. Elston was interviewed by the investigators, who asked him about the role of former Justice Department official Monica Goodling in politicizing the selection process. Elston told investigators he could not recall Goodling telling him to select lawyers who appeared to share Attorney General Alberto Gonzales' philosophy. Goodling testified before a House panel last year that she had told Elston he should identify such candidates. Goodling directed Elston to lead the selection committee in 2006. She and Elston have both left the Justice Department. She refused to be interviewed for the inspector general's report. As a result of the controversy, the hiring process was changed in 2007 to insulate hiring decisions from political considerations. Both Justice Department policy and federal law prohibit discrimination in hiring for career positions on the basis of political affiliations. The report did not find clear evidence that an earlier screening committee took political considerations into account. It says data from 2002 shows a disparity in the hiring of liberal and conservative candidates, but there were no complaints about the committee's work from 2003 to 2006, when Goodling put Elston in charge of the process. The report Tuesday is the first of perhaps several to be issued as the broad-ranging investigation into the role partisan politics has played in the Justice Department during the Bush administration. Goodling is expected to be a central figure in later inspector general reports examining efforts to increase the influence of conservatives in the department. The Justice Department Office of Professional Responsibility, a separate watchdog office that monitors prosecutorial conduct, joined in the inspector general's investigation. CNN's Terry Frieden contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Justice Department officials blocked liberals and individuals with ties to the Democratic Party from a highly selective program designed to channel young lawyers into government positions, according to an internal investigation released Tuesday.

The investigation found that bias against liberals existed within a Justice Department program intended to recruit young attorneys. Esther Slater McDonald, a political appointee at the department, “wrote disparaging statements about the candidates’ liberal and Democratic Party affiliations on the applications she reviewed and ... she voted to deselect candidates on that basis,” according to the report by Inspector General Glenn Fine.

McDonald, who has since left the department, refused to be interviewed for the investigation.

The report, the first official inquiry to document politicization within the Justice Department during the Bush administration, stems from a broader investigation into department politics prompted by the controversy over the firing of nine U.S. attorneys.

It found that two of the three members of a screening committee considered political views and experience when selecting new lawyers for the Justice Department Honors Program and Summer Law Intern Program.

The report concluded that McDonald and Michael Elston, chief of staff to Deputy Attorney General Paul McNulty, engaged in misconduct, an administrative violation. The third member of the screening committee, career attorney Dan Fridman, was cleared of any involvement in politicizing the process.

Elston was interviewed by investigators, who asked him about the role of former Justice Department official Monica Goodling in politicizing the selection process. Elston told investigators he could not recall Goodling instructing him to select lawyers who appeared to share Attorney General Alberto Gonzales’ philosophy.

Goodling testified before a House panel last year that she had told Elston he should identify such candidates. She directed Elston to lead the selection committee in 2006. Both Goodling and Elston have since left the Justice Department. Goodling refused to be interviewed for the inspector general’s report.

In response to the controversy, the hiring process was revised in 2007 to shield hiring decisions from political considerations. Both Justice Department policy and federal law prohibit discrimination in hiring for career positions on the basis of political affiliation.

The report did not find clear evidence that an earlier screening committee had considered political factors. It noted that data from 2002 showed a disparity in the hiring of liberal and conservative candidates, but that there were no complaints about the committee’s work from 2003 to 2006, when Goodling placed Elston in charge of the process.

Tuesday’s report is the first of what may be several findings issued as part of the wide-ranging investigation into the role partisan politics played in the Justice Department during the Bush administration.

Goodling is expected to be a central figure in later inspector general reports examining efforts to increase conservative influence within the department.

The Justice Department’s Office of Professional Responsibility, a separate watchdog office that monitors prosecutorial conduct, joined the inspector general’s investigation.

The investigation concluded that political bias against liberals affected a Justice Department program designed to recruit young lawyers. McDonald, who is no longer with the Justice Department, declined to speak with investigators.

The report is the first official inquiry to document politicization inside the Justice Department during the Bush administration. It stems from a broader investigation into political influence at the department, which began after controversy erupted over the dismissals of nine U.S. attorneys.

Investigators found that two of the three members of a screening panel took political ideology and experience into account when selecting new lawyers for the Justice Department Honors Program and the Summer Law Intern Program.

The report determined that McDonald and Michael Elston, who served as chief of staff to Deputy Attorney General Paul McNulty, committed misconduct, described as an administrative violation. The panel’s third member, career attorney Dan Fridman, was cleared of participating in any politicization of the selection process.

Elston agreed to be interviewed by investigators. They questioned him about former Justice Department official Monica Goodling’s role in injecting politics into the selection system. Elston said he did not remember Goodling instructing him to choose lawyers who seemed to share Attorney General Alberto Gonzales’ views. However, Goodling testified before a House committee the previous year that she had told Elston to look for such candidates.

Goodling assigned Elston to head the selection committee in 2006. Both Goodling and Elston have since left the Justice Department. Goodling refused to be interviewed for the inspector general’s report.

Following the controversy, the department revised its hiring procedures in 2007 to shield employment decisions from political influence. Justice Department rules and federal law both bar discrimination in hiring for career jobs based on political affiliation.

The report did not uncover clear proof that an earlier screening committee considered political factors. It noted that 2002 data showed an imbalance in the hiring of liberal and conservative applicants, but said there were no complaints about the committee’s work from 2003 through 2006, when Goodling placed Elston in charge of the process.

Tuesday’s report is expected to be the first of several arising from the wider investigation into the role partisan politics played in the Justice Department during the Bush administration. Goodling is likely to be a major subject in future inspector general reports examining attempts to expand conservative influence within the department.

The Justice Department’s Office of Professional Responsibility, a separate oversight office responsible for monitoring prosecutorial conduct, also participated in the inspector general’s investigation.

CNN’s Terry Frieden contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.output:
**Report: Bush-era Justice Department officials improperly screened out liberal applicants**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — A Justice Department inspector general report has found that officials in the Bush administration improperly used political and ideological considerations to screen applicants for two prestigious entry-level hiring programs, rejecting candidates with Democratic or liberal affiliations at a significantly higher rate than those with Republican or conservative ties.

The report, issued by the department’s inspector general and Office of Professional Responsibility, concluded that political appointees and some career officials violated federal law and Justice Department policy while reviewing applicants for the Attorney General’s Honors Program and the Summer Law Intern Program.

Those programs are among the department’s most competitive recruiting pipelines, drawing law students and recent graduates seeking positions in divisions such as civil rights, criminal enforcement, antitrust and national security.

Investigators found that during the 2002 and 2006 hiring cycles, officials looked at applicants’ political and ideological affiliations — including membership in groups such as the American Constitution Society, Democratic political campaigns, and organizations associated with civil rights or liberal causes — when deciding whether candidates should advance.

According to the report, applicants with liberal or Democratic credentials were disproportionately removed from consideration, while candidates with conservative or Republican affiliations were more likely to survive the screening process.

The inspector general said such conduct ran counter to longstanding department rules requiring that career hiring decisions be based on merit, not politics.

“The evidence showed that political or ideological affiliations were used to deselect candidates,” the report said, describing the practice as improper and contrary to department policy.

The report focused in part on a 2006 screening committee that included political appointees in the office of the deputy attorney general. Investigators said members of that committee searched résumés and applications for signs of political activity or ideological leanings. In some cases, the report found, notations were made about applicants’ affiliations with liberal organizations, Democratic lawmakers or advocacy groups.

Investigators also found evidence that conservative affiliations were treated more favorably. Applicants who had worked with the Federalist Society, Republican campaigns or conservative legal organizations were less likely to be rejected on political grounds, the report said.

The findings add to a series of controversies involving allegations that the Justice Department under President George W. Bush allowed political considerations to influence decisions traditionally handled by career professionals. The department had already faced scrutiny over the 2006 dismissals of several U.S. attorneys and accusations that political loyalty played a role in personnel decisions.

Justice Department officials said the practices described in the report were unacceptable and that new safeguards had been put in place to prevent political screening in career hiring.

The report recommended that the department clarify hiring rules, improve training for officials involved in recruitment and consider disciplinary action where appropriate. However, some of the officials cited had already left the department by the time the investigation was completed, limiting potential disciplinary measures.

Democrats in Congress said the findings confirmed concerns that the Bush administration had politicized parts of the Justice Department. Republicans criticized any improper political screening but said the conduct described did not reflect the work of the department as a whole.

The inspector general emphasized that career positions at the Justice Department must remain insulated from partisan influence, noting that public confidence in federal law enforcement depends on the perception that hiring and decision-making are based on qualifications and the rule of law.

“The department must ensure that political or ideological considerations play no role in career hiring,” the report said.

**Justice watchdog: Political appointees improperly screened DOJ applicants for Democratic, liberal ties**

**WASHINGTON —** Political appointees at the Justice Department improperly used job candidates’ Democratic Party or liberal affiliations to influence hiring decisions for career positions, violating federal law and department policy, according to a report by the department’s inspector general.

The report found that officials in the Justice Department during the Bush administration considered political and ideological factors when evaluating applicants for some nonpolitical jobs, including career attorney posts. Candidates whose résumés or applications reflected ties to Democratic elected officials, liberal advocacy groups or progressive causes were disadvantaged, while applicants with Republican or conservative credentials were favored, investigators concluded.

The findings marked another chapter in the long-running controversy over politicization inside the Justice Department, which intensified after the 2006 firings of U.S. attorneys and led to congressional investigations, resignations of senior officials and repeated pledges by department leaders to restore confidence in the agency’s independence.

The inspector general’s office said the hiring practices violated the Civil Service Reform Act and Justice Department rules, which generally prohibit the consideration of political affiliation in hiring for career government jobs. Career positions are supposed to be filled on the basis of merit, not partisan loyalty.

“Political or ideological affiliations were used to assess candidates for career positions,” the report concluded, saying that such considerations had “no place” in the selection process for nonpolitical Justice Department posts.

Investigators reviewed e-mails, applications and witness interviews and found that political appointees screened candidates for signs of partisan or ideological leanings. In some cases, applicants were rejected or downgraded after reviewers noted their work for Democratic lawmakers, liberal public-interest organizations or groups associated with civil rights, women’s rights, gay rights, environmental causes or other progressive issues.

The report said the practice affected hiring for competitive career slots, including entry-level and summer legal positions, and contributed to a selection process that was tilted away from applicants perceived as liberal or Democratic. The watchdog found that some officials searched applications for political clues and treated those clues as negatives.

The report did not conclude that every hiring decision was tainted, and it did not identify a precise number of candidates who would have been hired absent the improper screening. But it said the evidence showed a pattern in which political and ideological considerations were inserted into what should have been a merit-based process.

Justice Department officials said they accepted the report’s findings and had taken steps to prevent similar conduct, including changes to hiring procedures and training for employees involved in recruitment. Department leaders said political affiliation is not an appropriate factor in hiring career employees.

The inspector general’s findings renewed criticism from Democrats in Congress, who said the report confirmed that partisan loyalty tests had been used inside the nation’s top law enforcement agency.

“This was not simply bad judgment,” critics said. “It was an abuse of the public trust.”

Republican officials have generally argued that the misconduct was limited to a small number of appointees and that corrective action had already been taken.

The report is one of several internal reviews examining whether political considerations influenced Justice Department personnel decisions during the Bush years. Earlier inquiries scrutinized the dismissal of U.S. attorneys and the role of senior officials in personnel decisions affecting prosecutors, immigration judges and other department employees.

The inspector general’s office said the improper hiring practices damaged the department’s credibility and risked undermining public confidence that Justice Department lawyers act independently of partisan interests.

Because some of the officials involved had left government service, the report said disciplinary options were limited. The watchdog referred certain findings to department officials for possible action and recommended additional safeguards to ensure that career hiring decisions remain insulated from politics.

The Justice Department’s career workforce includes prosecutors, litigators, immigration judges, trial attorneys and other lawyers who are expected to serve across administrations. Federal rules distinguish those positions from political appointments, which are filled by presidential appointees and other officials who may be chosen based in part on policy alignment.

The report said that distinction was blurred when political appointees injected partisan screening into career hiring.

“Using political affiliation as a factor in career hiring undermines the merit system,” the watchdog concluded. “It deprives applicants of fair consideration and compromises the integrity of the Department of Justice.”

**Justice Department Overhauls Entry-Level Lawyer Hiring After Watchdog Finds Political Screening**

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Justice Department changed the way it hires young lawyers after internal watchdogs found that officials improperly screened applicants for the department’s prestigious Honors Program and summer law intern positions based on political and ideological views, including evidence that candidates were evaluated for conservative affiliations or beliefs.

The changes followed findings by the Justice Department’s Office of the Inspector General and Office of Professional Responsibility that, during the George W. Bush administration, some officials involved in hiring considered factors such as party ties, membership in political or ideological organizations, and applicants’ perceived views on issues such as abortion, same-sex marriage and gun rights. The watchdogs concluded that such considerations violated federal civil service rules and department policy, which require career attorney hiring to be based on merit rather than political affiliation.

At issue were the Attorney General’s Honors Program, the department’s main entry-level hiring path for law graduates and judicial clerks, and the Summer Law Intern Program, a key pipeline for future department lawyers. Both programs are highly competitive and have traditionally been run as career hiring processes, not political appointments.

According to the watchdog report, political appointees and senior officials played an unusually active role in screening applications in certain years, rejecting or advancing candidates after reviewing résumés for clues about ideology. Applicants associated with groups viewed as liberal or Democratic were sometimes marked down, while candidates with conservative credentials could receive favorable treatment. Investigators found that some screeners searched the internet for information about applicants’ political activity and made notes reflecting political or ideological judgments.

In response, the Justice Department revised the hiring process to reduce the role of political appointees and strengthen oversight by career officials. The department moved to ensure that applications for the Honors Program and summer intern program would be reviewed under standardized, merit-based criteria, with hiring decisions tied to qualifications such as academic achievement, legal experience, writing ability, clerkships and demonstrated commitment to public service.

The department also implemented additional training for employees involved in hiring, emphasizing that political affiliation and ideology may not be used in selecting career attorneys. Officials were instructed to document hiring decisions more carefully, preserve records, and follow procedures designed to prevent improper considerations from entering the process.

The reforms were intended to restore confidence in the department’s career hiring system, which had been damaged by the watchdog findings. The Honors Program has long been viewed as one of the most important gateways into federal public service for new lawyers, feeding talent into divisions that handle civil rights, national security, antitrust, tax, criminal enforcement and other major legal work.

Justice Department leaders said the revised process was designed to ensure that entry-level lawyers are selected fairly and without political litmus tests. The watchdogs also recommended that the department consider disciplinary action for officials found to have used improper criteria, though several had already left government service by the time the findings were released.

The episode became part of a broader controversy over politicization at the Justice Department during the Bush administration, including allegations that political considerations influenced personnel decisions in other parts of the department. The hiring changes were meant to draw a clearer line between political leadership, which sets policy, and career legal positions, which are supposed to be filled through nonpartisan, merit-based procedures.
